taxonomic_note: Accepted by Kew/POWO; native in Texas. Historical synonyms include Poa trichodes, Eragrostis pilifera, and E. trichodes var. pilifera.
look_here_first: Look for an erect perennial tuft with long loose arching leaves and a very large, diffuse mature panicle. On a leafy stem examine LONG HAIRS at the SHEATH THROAT, a short hair-fringe ligule and usually glabrous nodes; then examine where small spikelets sit along the very slender branching stalks. Do not separate from plains or bigtop solely by panicle size.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays County regional report lists sand lovegrass among natural grasses found in the Hays County study area. UT Plant Resources Center has a Williamson County field treatment. Kerr Wildlife Management Area vascular checklist includes Eragrostis trichodes.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Candidate seed mixes were not counted as native-county evidence.

best_field_traits: long hairs concentrated at sheath throat/collar
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Eragrostis intermedia: Usually shorter with mostly smooth sheaths and a smaller airy panicle. Eragrostis hirsuta: Hirsute across sheath surface with bearded panicle axils rather than collar-focused long hairs. Eragrostis cilianensis: Annual, coarser, glandular and many-flowered.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Sand lovegrass combines a relatively tall persistent tuft, arching foliage and a large airy oblong panicle with throat-focused long hairs. Plains lovegrass is often shorter with less shaggy sheath body and a smaller panicle; bigtop typically bears more extensive sheath hairiness. Stinkgrass is an annual with coarser glandular reproductive parts. None of these is guaranteed from a lone distant view.

field_id_finish_pass.level: PHOTO_LED_TEACHING_PASS — diagnostic collar and mature spikelet macro needed
field_id_finish_pass.looked_at: Both physically installed Sam Kieschnick photos checked 2026-10-20: one depicts pale tiny spikelets on almost hairlike branches in fingers, the other a loose tuft in an open disturbed site. The photos do not prove sheath-throat or node hair condition.
field_id_finish_pass.crew_summary: This is the tall wispy lovegrass. Look at the whole base and seedhead, then go straight to the sheath throat and a mature spikelet before you call sand lovegrass.
lookalike_logic: Plains: both airy, but sand is often a taller arching tuft with conspicuous throat hair tufts.
Bigtop: hairs along sheath body/margins much more extensive; sand tends to concentrate at sheath mouth.
Purple: the cloud can be colored but has strongly spreading flexible branches, may tumble.
Stinkgrass: annual and generally coarser spikelets with possible conspicuous glands.
difficult_id_guardrails: No sheath-throat closeup or ligule closeup in current inspected pair; don't label hair location as photographed.
A hair-thin panicle alone is not species-proof; source observations may be provisionally identified.
Avoid cultivar exemplars for local wild-species key; comparison photos are noncultivar sourced records.
Preserve previously recorded native target-zone evidence unchanged.
field_id_finish_pass.publish_check: Canonical photo-led teaching and source-photo annotations only; no new photo binary or claim of active Pages deployment.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Sand lovegrass: whole tuft, fine spikelets, then throat hairs
steps: At a distance, photograph the arching perennial clump and the complete panicle.
In the hand-held closeup, pick out ONE small spikelet on a thin branch/pedicel, instead of treating the whole cloud as a single structure.
At the sheath mouth, use a hand lens to document the long throat hairs, true hair-fringe ligule and glabrous culm node; no existing photo here shows these reliably.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: The current card can train panicle and tuft recognition, but species-level confidence requires collar/node and mature spikelet views.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: No arrows imply the throat hairs, ligule or node are visible in today's image set.
